bib.title: Dr. Zero: Self-Evolving Search Agents without Training Data

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Dr. Zero: Self-Evolving Search Agents without Training Data", Zhenrui Yue, Kartikeya Upasani, Xianjun Yang, Suyu Ge, Shaoliang Nie, Yuning Mao, Zhe Liu, Dong Wang (Meta Superintelligence Labs, UIUC). arXiv:2601.07055v2, dated July 2026 (v2, 21 Jul 2026). Preprint. Code: github.com/facebookresearch/drzero

COVERAGE: All 26 pages, 82,381 chars. I read the body, conclusion, and appendix A.1 to A.3 (hyperparameters, ablations, HRPO vs GRPO, cost, significance tests). I skimmed the references, and I only skimmed the prompt and example figures (Figs 5-14) that follow A.3 (about line 720 on). Extraction was clean.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Dr.Zero, trained with no human QA data, roughly matches the supervised Search-R1 on average at 3B. At 7B it is slightly behind (0.372 vs 0.384).
  number: 3B avg 0.326 vs 0.327; 7B avg 0.372 vs 0.384
  setup: Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct, 7 QA benchmarks (NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle), exact match, greedy decoding, E5-base retriever, English Wikipedia dump, top-3 passages. Table 1 is the 7B result after iteration 2, because the iteration-3 7B average is 0.360.
  quote: "Search-R1 0.323 0.537 0.3640.308 0.336 0.105 0.3150.327 / Dr. Zero 0.397 0.572 0.431 0.298 0.291 0.091 0.200 0.326"
  where: Table 1, p.6
- claim: At 3B, Dr.Zero beats Search-R1 on the one-hop sets. At 7B it reaches about 90% of Search-R1 on multi-hop but wins on 2WikiMQA. Search-R1 stays ahead on MuSiQue and Bamboogle.
  number: +22.9% NQ, +6.5% TriviaQA, +18.4% PopQA (3B); about 90% (7B multi-hop)
  setup: Table 1. The percentages are relative, and these are single greedy runs.
  quote: "our 3B model outperforms the supervised Search-R1 by 22.9%, 6.5% and 18.4% respectively. In complex multi-hop scenarios, the 7B variant achieves roughly 90% of Search-R1's performance and even outperforms it on the challenging 2WikiMQA."
  where: p.7
- claim: Dr.Zero clearly beats the earlier data-free methods once those are given multi-turn search.
  number: +39.9% over SQLM*, +27.3% over R-Zero* (average); +83.3% over R-Zero* on the four multi-hop sets
  setup: 3B, Table 2. Averages: SQLM* 0.233, R-Zero* 0.256, Dr.Zero 0.326. The authors augmented the baselines themselves (the asterisk).
  quote: "It exceeds SQLM* and R-Zero* by an average of 39.9% and 27.3% respectively." and "Dr.Zero yields an average relative gain of 83.3% over R-Zero* across the four multi-hop benchmarks."
  where: p.7
- claim: Earlier data-free proposers collapse to one-hop questions. This is the paper's motivation for forcing a hop mix.
  number: 93.4% and 95.6% one-hop
  setup: 500 generated questions each from SQLM* and R-Zero*, hop structure labelled by gemini-3-flash-preview. Dr.Zero's default 4:3:2:1 hop ratio gives 60% of seed prompts two to four hops.
  quote: "One-hop questions account for 93.4% and 95.6% of their respective outputs, confirming a strong bias toward structurally simple questions."
  where: A.2, p.16
- claim: HRPO needs 6 rollouts per proposer prompt instead of 20, which cuts cost and gives a slightly better average score than nested GRPO.
  number: 6 vs 20 rollouts; 4.16h vs 10.58h; 33.28 vs 84.64 GPU-hours; GPU utilisation 21.63% vs 17.84%; average EM 0.326 vs 0.320
  setup: 3B proposer training per iteration on one 8xH100 node. GRPO baseline uses 4 questions x 4 predictions per prompt. HRPO uses 1 question and 5 solver predictions.
  quote: "HRPO 6 (1 question + 5 predictions) 4.16h 33.28 21.63% / GRPO 20 (4 questions + 16 predictions) 10.58h 84.64 17.84%" and "HRPO achieves an average score of 0.326, even surpassing the 0.320 baseline of GRPO."
  where: Tables 8-9, p.16
- claim: HRPO's gain over GRPO is on one-hop sets. GRPO is better on multi-hop sets (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, Bamboogle). The authors concede that hard multi-step tasks may still need the extra compute for accurate baselines.
  number: Bamboogle 0.200 (HRPO) vs 0.272 (GRPO); NQ 0.397 vs 0.361
  setup: 3B, Table 8
  quote: "HRPO demonstrates superior performance on one-hop datasets (e.g., NQ), while GRPO retains an advantage on multi-hop benchmarks (e.g., HotpotQA)."
  where: p.16
- claim: Self-evolution saturates within 2-3 iterations. The 7B model gets worse at iteration 3 and shows training instability.
  number: 3B avg 0.304 -> 0.319 -> 0.326; 7B avg 0.366 -> 0.372 -> 0.360
  setup: Table 3, each iteration is 50 proposer steps plus 50 solver steps. The default is 3 iterations (150 steps per model).
  quote: "the 7B model drops slightly from 0.372 to 0.360, indicating a performance plateau." Also "inconsistent token IDs across multi-turn search and reasoning steps" is named as the most common failure mode.
  where: p.8
- claim: In the 3B ablations, removing the seed document hurts most, and the pass-rate difficulty reward beats a parabolic reward.
  number: avg 0.304 (full) vs 0.245 (no initial document) vs 0.289 (no format reward); 100 steps gives 0.302
  setup: 3B, a single iteration of 50 steps (Table 7). The averages are the paper's text, computed from the table.
  quote: "The most significant performance drop occurs when the initial document is removed (average score falls to 0.245)." and "Removing the format reward results in an average performance drop from 0.304 to 0.289"
  where: A.2, p.15
- claim: A mixed hop curriculum is best. For 3B, more multi-hop questions did not help, so the paper suggests basic search skill matters for small models.
  number: avg 0.314 (1:1:1:1), 0.316 (2:1:1:1), 0.326 (4:3:2:1) at 3B; 0.368, 0.369, 0.372 at 7B
  setup: Table 4, hop ratios 1/2/3/4-hop.
  quote: "performance depends on balancing questions across hop levels rather than simply maximizing the proportion of multi-hop questions."
  where: p.9
- claim: Across repeated runs the 7B model's gain on 2WikiMQA is significant, and 3B's gain on NQ is significant. Table 1 itself is single-run greedy.
  number: +7.67% relative on 2WikiMQA (7B); 7B 2WikiMQA 0.351±.007 vs 0.326
  setup: Table 10, mean ± std over runs (the run count is not stated in the extraction).
  quote: "achieving a significant 7.67% relative improvement on 2WikiMQA."
  where: p.17

METHOD (for the note)
- Two agents start from the same base LLM. Both are search agents, using only a search tool and no demonstrations or human questions.
- The proposer gets a seed document, searches, and emits a question and an answer. The solver then attempts the question n times.
- Proposer reward (Eq 4): r = I(0<k<n)·(n−k)/(n−1) + r_f, where k is the number of correct solver answers out of n. It is maximal when exactly one attempt is correct and decays linearly, with 0 for all-correct or all-wrong. r_f is a format reward, with a max of 0.5 over 4 parts: think tags, valid tool use, question tag, answer tag.
- HRPO (Eq 3): the advantage is standardised within the group of questions with the same hop count h: A = (r_i − mean_h)/(sqrt(var_h)+δ). There is one question per seed and no nested sampling. Hop count is only a grouping variable, and difficulty comes from the solver pass rate. Strictly on-policy, no ratio clipping, KL coefficient 0.
- The solver is trained with ordinary GRPO on exact-match outcome reward against the proposer's synthetic answer.
- The loop alternates, 50 proposer steps then 50 solver steps, for up to 3 iterations. Group size is 5, batch 256, max 5 turns.
- The authors found that a global baseline (REINFORCE++) was unstable on mixed query structures.
- Quote: "we find that a global baseline becomes unstable when processing diverse query structures."

LIMITS
- Short-form, verifiable QA only. Exact-match on Wikipedia with a fixed E5 retriever and a single corpus. The authors say gains are not separated from reasoning over retrieved passages.
- Only Qwen2.5 3B/7B. Table 1 is single-run greedy, with variance only in Table 10 (A.2). No parity at 7B (0.372 vs 0.384); Search-R1 wins on MuSiQue and Bamboogle.
- Synthetic answers can be wrong or ambiguous. The authors say the grounding rules "reduce, but do not eliminate" this.
- The 7B model plateaus or regresses by iteration 3. There are token-ID inconsistency failures in multi-turn training. Entropy collapse and reward hacking or bias amplification are left as future work.
- HRPO is weaker than GRPO on multi-hop sets. The ablations are 3B, one iteration only. The data-free baselines are the authors' own multi-turn re-implementations (SQLM*, R-Zero*).
- The search tool the proposer uses is the same corpus used at evaluation.

BUILDS ON: R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025a, proposer-solver co-evolution); SQLM (Chen et al., 2025, self-questioning); GRPO (Shao et al., 2024); Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025, the supervised baseline); REINFORCE++ (Hu, 2025); Ahmadian et al. 2024 (REINFORCE-style); DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025); IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023); Search-o1 (Li et al., 2025); RAG (Lewis et al., 2020); Search Self-Play (Lu et al., 2025, concurrent); SPICE (Liu et al., 2025b); verl implementation; E5 (Wang et al., 2022).

CODE: none in the paper. Only the Eq (3) and (4) definitions above, plus prompts in Figures 5-6. Repo is facebookresearch/drzero.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.2): the R-Zero-style proposer/solver loop, background only.
- Fig 2 (p.4): the Dr.Zero loop. The proposer is updated with HRPO using difficulty rewards, and the solver with GRPO using outcome rewards. This is the best picture of the method.
- Fig 3 (p.8): proposer and solver reward curves per iteration.
- Fig 4 (p.9): entropy and response length during 3B training.
- Fig 5/6: proposer and solver prompts. Figs 7-14: example trajectories, with the last example of each kind shown as a failure.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure captions came from the text extraction only; I did not run the figures script. The run count behind the Table 10 standard deviations is not stated in the text I read. Exact bold/underline markings in Tables 1 and 3 are garbled in extraction, so the "best" cells cannot be trusted. The figure text of the prompts (Figs 5-14) was not read closely.
